outline.description: Sets the stage for why few‐shot tabular learning remains challenging, how large language models bring a unique prior knowledge resource, and outlines the main aim of turning an LLM into an efficient feature engineer.
subtopics: Motivation behind studying very low‑label regimes in structured data
Limitations of existing end‑to‑end LLM predictors (per‑sample inference cost, prompt size limits)
"FeatLLM" idea: let an LLM generate decision criteria instead of raw predictions
High‑level pipeline overview – reasoning → rule extraction → binary‐feature creation → lightweight downstream classifier
Key claims and empirical gains reported against state‑of‑the‑art baselines

outline.description: Places the contribution among two main research streams – classic few‐shot learning on tabular data and recent effort integrating language models into structured‐data pipelines.
subtopics: Few‐shot learning fundamentals – transfer priors vs unlabeled augmentation
"TabPFN", "SCARF", "STUNT" and other prototypical approaches
"Language‐Interfaced" methods: serialising tables → prompts ↔ sampling techniques ↔ finetune strategies
Limitations shared by existing works (heavy inference load, lack of interpretability, poor scaling with long tables)
"FeatLLM" positioning relative to In‐context Learning, TABLET, TabLLM

outline.description: Precisely describes the supervised classification setting adopted throughout the paper together with formal notation used later.
subtopics:
"D = \{(x^i , y^i )\}_{i=1}^{N}"” definition (
• “x” d-dimensional vector
• “y” one‑hot label vector
• feature name set “F = {f_j }” available in natural language
• only k labelled samples are kept during training
)
"k–shot" regime definition k << N and its implications
'Rule extraction → binary vector z_c^i construction’ roadmap through which this section reserves mathematical symbols

outline.description: Explains how the authors construct specialised prompts that enable an LLM’s reasoning pathway toward interpretable hypothesis testing.
subtopics: "Basic information description": task wording (“Does … ?”, column typology diagrams)
"Serialization scheme" converting every record into a sentence → the stripped format used mostly in prior work
"Reasoning instruction": two‐step chain‐of‐thought forcing first an abstract causal view then concrete classly tailored rules
"Response instruction": strict YAMLish form so every rule begins with ‘ruleX : …’ facilitating downstream parser
'Example excerpts’ hierarchy displayed in Fig 1 / Appendix showing synthetic prompt artefacts

outline.description: Describes how naturally generated prose is converted back into executable predicates without manual preprocessing.
subtopics: 'Noisy syntax’: why traditional regex fails when operators get verbalized (“greater than” → “>”)
'Self-consistent code generation': passing crafted function templates back through the same model yields compact Python stubs
'exec()’ mechanics’: evaluating client code locally gives a boolean matrix indicating equivalence between sample context and extracted rules
'Security/about reproducibility': noting intentional lightweight sandbox environment discussed briefly

outline.chapter_title: Rule–Based Binary Features And Lightweight Classifier
outline.description: Introduces the central modelling idea where previously discovered rules become an interpretable “feature bank’’ subsequently fed through a constrained linear map.
subtopics: 'Rule pool': Z_c^i ∈ {0, 1}^R counts satisfied conditions per class r=numberOfRulesPerClass
'Positive weighting scheme': WO′ = max(WO ,0) guarantees every learned coefficient lifts likelihood instead of suppressing
'Softmax over logits': turning weighted sums into calibrated probabilities
'Training regime': Adam(η=0.01), up to 200 epochs , cross entropy loss optimisation conducted solely on k labelled examples
'Alternative naïve scoring': counting flags without tuning highlighted later with ablations

outline.description: Explains how repeatedly sampling prompts creates diverse weak learners whose consensus erodes variance caused by noisy rules while easing batch size limits.
\"Key mechanisms\": variable temperature: 'Resampling LaP along with higher temperature introduces independent candidates differing both syntactically & semantically'
'Special case handling when table width exceeds token budget'
'Final prediction computation’: averages ensembled softmax outputs yielding smoother calibration'
